:::{#def-angle}
#### Angle between two vectors

The **angle** between two nonzero vectors $\vecf{x}, \vecf{y} \in \reals^p$
is the unique number $\angpar \in [0, \pi]$ whose cosine (@def-cosine-sine) satisfies

$$
\cos\angpar = \frac{\vecf{x} \cdot \vecf{y}}{\norm{\vecf{x}}\,\norm{\vecf{y}}}.
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-angle-well-defined}
#### Why the angle is well defined

The denominator is positive, because both vectors are nonzero (@thm-norm-properties),
and by @thm-cauchy-schwarz the ratio lies between $-1$ and $1$.
On $[0, \pi]$, $\cos$ is decreasing from $1$ to $-1$
and takes each value in $[-1, 1]$ exactly once,
so there is exactly one such $\angpar$.
The angle is $\pi/2$ exactly when $\vecf{x} \cdot \vecf{y} = 0$,
so for nonzero vectors, orthogonal (@def-orthogonal-vectors) means at a right angle.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-angle}
#### Some angles in the plane

- $(1, 0)$ and $(1, 1)$:
  $\cos\angpar = \frac{1}{1 \cd \sqrt{2}}$, so $\angpar = \pi/4$.
- $(1, 2)$ and $(-2, 1)$:

  $$
  \begin{aligned}
  \cos\angpar &= \frac{-2 + 2}{\sqrt{5}\,\sqrt{5}} \\
  &= 0,
  \end{aligned}
  $$

  so $\angpar = \pi/2$.
- $(1, 0)$ and $(-3, 0)$:

  $$
  \begin{aligned}
  \cos\angpar &= \frac{-3}{1 \cd 3} \\
  &= -1,
  \end{aligned}
  $$

  so $\angpar = \pi$.
- $(1, 0)$ and $\vzero$: there is no angle,
  because the ratio would divide by $\norm{\vzero} = 0$.

:::
